extracted.intended_audience: Citizens, state legislators, and readers debating ratification of the U.S. Constitution (people of New York and the broader public)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and argumentative standards for structuring federal elections and legislative representation—allocation of regulatory power between states and the Union, appropriate size and function of representative bodies, quorum rules, and safeguards against factional or elite capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient but not excessive number of representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: AFTER SECURING A SUFFICIENT NUMBER FOR THE PURPOSES OF SAFETY, OF LOCAL INFORMATION, AND OF DIFFUSIVE SYMPATHY WITH THE WHOLE SOCIETY, they will counteract their own views by every addition to their representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not multiply representatives beyond the point needed for safety, local knowledge, and broad sympathy; very large assemblies increase the ascendency of passion over reason, raise the proportion of members of limited information, and enable the eloquence and address of a few to dominate. The more numerous an assembly, the fewer the men who in fact will direct proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: House control of the purse as an effective safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Representatives ... hold the purse that powerful instrument ... may, in fact, be regarded as the most complete and effectual weapon ... for obtaining a redress of every grievance, and for carrying into effect every just and salutary measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design lower-house control of supplies/appropriations to function as a constitutional check: even if the Senate resists, the House's power over money can secure redress and implement measures. This power provides practical leverage for the popular branch to defend its rights and policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quorum and majority rules should not be elevated above a simple majority
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been said that more than a majority ought to have been required for a quorum; and in particular cases, if not in all, more than a majority of a quorum for a decision. ... But these considerations are outweighed by the inconveniences in the opposite scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring a quorum or decisions greater than a simple majority shifts decisive power to minorities, can obstruct justice or necessary measures, permits interested minorities to shield themselves from equitable sacrifices, and fosters secessionist practices. Prefer majority-rule quorums to avoid transferring power to minorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every government must contain means of its own preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: EVERY GOVERNMENT OUGHT TO CONTAIN IN ITSELF THE MEANS OF ITS OWN PRESERVATION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design should include internal mechanisms (including reservation of certain powers) enabling the national government to protect its existence. Where practical change over time is likely, some discretionary national authority is necessary to preserve the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve to Congress the ultimate power to regulate TIMES, PLACES, and MANNER of federal elections (with specified exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: The TIMES, PLACES, and MANNER of holding elections for senators and representatives shall be prescribed in each State ... but the Congress may, at any time, by law, make or alter SUCH REGULATIONS, except as to the PLACES of choosing senators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give initial regulatory control to states for convenience and local satisfaction, but reserve to the national legislature a power to interpose when extraordinary circumstances threaten national safety. This balance combines local administration with a constitutional ultimate safeguard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving exclusive control of federal election regulation to State legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be more evident, than that an exclusive power of regulating elections for the national government, in the hands of the State legislatures, would leave the existence of the Union entirely at their mercy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not vest exclusive authority in state legislatures to regulate federal elections: they could neglect or manipulate elections to destroy the Union. Even if practical neglect seems unlikely, the constitutional possibility of such abuse is an unanswerable objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: National power over time/places/manner is procedural and cannot alter qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority would be expressly restricted to the regulation of the TIMES, the PLACES, the MANNER of elections. The qualifications of the persons who may choose or be chosen ... are defined and fixed in the Constitution, and are unalterable by the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning the national legislature power over election procedure, explicitly limit that power to procedural aspects so it cannot be used to alter voter or candidate qualifications (e.g., property qualifications). Structural protections for qualifications must remain immutable by ordinary statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbability and impracticality of using procedural regulation to favor a particular class
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all chimerical suppositions, this seems to be the most chimerical ... if so improper a spirit should ever gain admittance into [national councils], it would display itself in a form altogether different and far more decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims that Congress could use time/place/manner rules to elevate 'the wealthy and the well-born' as unrealistic: such maneuvers would provoke popular revolt, and the national government's mixed composition (House, Senate, President) makes a durable, systematic bias unlikely. Structural diversity in government reduces the risk of sustained partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confining places of election is a poor instrument for elite preference and risks disenfranchisement
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no method of securing to the rich the preference apprehended, but by prescribing qualifications of property ... This forms no part of the power to be conferred upon the national government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting places of election to particular spots will not reliably concentrate elite power (wealthy persons are scattered), and, if inconvenient, will deter remote electors—whether at state or national level—thus risking de facto disenfranchisement. True exclusion requires altering qualifications, which is not permitted by times/places/manner power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate structure mitigates risk of temporary state coalitions disrupting the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The senators are to be chosen for the period of six years; there is to be a rotation ... and no State is to be entitled to more than two senators; a quorum of the body is to consist of sixteen members. ... a temporary combination of a few States to intermit the appointment of senators, could neither annul the existence nor impair the activity of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the upper chamber with longer terms, staggered rotation, equal small state representation, and a relatively modest quorum to make it resilient to temporary conspiracies or conspiratorial omissions by a few state legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link reapportionment and augmentation to build cross-state coalitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The large States ... will have nothing to do but to make reapportionments and augmentations mutually conditions of each other; and the senators from all the most growing States will be bound to contend for the latter, by the interest which their States will feel in the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use institutional linkage—tying reapportionment (which benefits growing states) to augmentation of representatives—to create incentives for senators from rapidly growing states to support increases in House representation. This provides a practical mechanism to secure cooperation between House majorities and senators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish the people's interest from local rulers' interest when allocating powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The people of America may be warmly attached to the government of the Union, at times when the particular rulers of particular States ... may be in a very opposite temper. This diversity of sentiment ... is exemplified in some of the States at the present moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning authority over federal matters (like elections), account for the potential divergence between popular attachment to the Union and the ambitions or rivalries of state-level rulers; institutional safeguards at the national level help prevent state officials from using election power for personal aggrandizement or factional ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical equivalence of inconvenient election locations at state and federal levels
rubrics_metrics.description: When the place of election is at an INCONVENIENT DISTANCE from the elector, the effect upon his conduct will be the same whether that distance be twenty miles or twenty thousand miles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that appointment of inconvenient election sites reduces turnout similarly whether made by state or national authorities; objections to national regulation on this ground apply equally to many state constitutions and do not justify denying national procedural authority.
